rationale:
Evidence: iteration 5 is the best design so far (score 606.2). Oval finishes 20 of 20 (mean 1.98 s), so the controller works on gentle bends. S-bend finishes 11 of 20 (progress 0.96, mean finish 2.51 s), so it is close to completing. Slalom never finishes (0 of 20, mean progress 0.44, 1.15 line-loss events per run), and it is the largest source of lost score. Steering oscillation on s-bend (0.38) and slalom (0.23) is moderate. Iteration 4 to 5 showed that raising kp together with kd (4.0/0.6 to 4.5/0.8) improved progress without a large oscillation penalty. Slalom is limited by slow response to rapid direction changes, not by jitter.

Changes (controller only, geometry unchanged so the effect is isolated): (1) kp 4.5 to 4.8 for more steering authority on fast alternating bends. (2) kd 0.8 to 0.9 to keep the extra proportional gain damped, since kp 5 with kd 0.3 previously overshot. (3) ki 0.5 and base_speed 1.3 are unchanged, because the integral term is removing the motor-mismatch bias and the oval and s-bend timings still fit the 3 s limit.

Expected result: slalom progress rises above 0.5, with a first slalom completion possible. S-bend completions hold at about 50% or better. Oval stays at 20 of 20.

Hypotheses: (a) kd 0.9 keeps steering_oscillation on s-bend at or below 0.4 despite the higher kp, so kd is damping rather than adding lag. (b) If oval completion drops or oval steering_oscillation exceeds 0.35, kp 4.8 is too aggressive and should return toward 4.5. Measurements wanted next: completion and completion_time by track, progress and max_error on slalom and s-bend (to locate where the robot leaves the line), line_loss_events and rms_error (to judge kp), and steering_oscillation (to judge kd).
